Title: Love/Caring
Description: affection/warmth, beauty, closeness/touch, companionship, compassion, kindness, intimacy, mattering, importance, nurturing, sexual connection, respect, honoring, valuing/prizing
Strategies: Call a friend,Snuggle a pet,Cuddle your favorite stuffed animal,Self holding
Original Claim: Affectionate, reliable bonds support development and stress recovery across the lifespan. This need motivates warmth, protection, responsiveness, and generosity. Caring relationships are a durable pathway to health and meaning.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6318977/ (developmental psychology review: consistent loving caregiving in childhood improves emotional and physiological regulation into adulthood)
https://longevity.stanford.edu/lifestyle-medicine-2-relationships/ (Stanford Center on Longevity: strong loving relationships correlate with better health outcomes, stress reduction, and life satisfaction)
Rewritten Claim: Humans need to love and be loved – enduring bonds of affection and care are a major source of emotional nourishment and resilience throughout life. From infancy (where a caregiver’s love aids healthy brain and emotional development) to old age (where close loved ones buffer stress and give meaning), caring relationships consistently benefit our well-being. This need for love and caring drives behaviors like warmth (showing affection and kindness), protection (keeping loved ones safe), responsive listening and comfort, and acts of generosity toward those we care about. Studies have repeatedly shown that people embedded in reliable, loving relationships tend to recover faster from illness or stress and often live longer, happier lives than those who lack such bonds. In essence, caring relationships – whether with family, friends, or romantic partners – provide a lifelong foundation for health, stress relief, and a sense of meaning or purpose.

Title: Nurturing
Description: The desire to see life prosper. It can bring up great pain when our need for nurturing is not being met. We might think somehow we are to blame. Sometimes when we see suffering in other living things we experience pain that they are not being cared for or nurtured well. We might also feel it in us when someone’s behavior did not meet our need to be nurtured and/or considered.
Strategies: Call a parent,Snuggle a pet,Tend to a plant
Original Claim: Providing and receiving care maintains the capacity of individuals and communities. This need motivates offering support, inviting rest, and resourcing recovery. Nurturing replenishes systems so they remain workable over time.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13698575.2018.1545074 (study on community care systems: when people nurture and support each other, overall community resilience is higher)
https://www.apa.org/helpcenter/resilience (APA on resilience: having nurturant support (social support, time to rest and heal) is a key factor in bouncing back from adversity)
Rewritten Claim: Nurturing refers to the acts of caring for others (and allowing oneself to be cared for) that keep individuals and communities healthy and functional. Just as a caregiver nourishes a child, people of all ages need periods of support, rest, and recovery to stay at their best. This need for nurturing drives behaviors like offering help or comfort to those who are tired or struggling, encouraging breaks and rest periods, and supplying resources (emotional or material) to aid someone’s recovery from stress or illness. In a broader sense, a community that values nurturing will have structures (like supportive friendships, mentorship, healthcare services) that “recharge” its members regularly. Research on resilience underscores that those who have strong nurturing support systems (people who care for them, opportunities to recuperate) can handle difficulties without burning out. Providing consistent care ensures that both individuals and the larger group don’t get depleted – it replenishes energy and morale so that life or work remains sustainable over time.

Title: Connection
Description: I find connection to be a kind of doorway into the experience of another. We want to make contact with what is most real in one another. How powerful it is to experience connection with another person and how surprising it can be to experience connection within oneself. I find sometimes that when I listen careful for what is alive in me, when I make contact with that need that so wants to be seen, I experience a kind of connection within myself. Depression is often a kind of isolation from one’s own needs. We often experience the same kind of pain when we find ourselves isolated from what is alive in another person. We so want to be let in, to be invited in.
Strategies: Call a friend,Play a social video game,Read a character driven novel,One kind text,Specific thank-you

Title: Belonging
Description: What a profound experience it can be to have our need for belonging met and how profoundly painful it can be to have it going unmet. We so want to be known as we are, to be seen completely, and accepted. We want to know we have a place in this world. We want to know that we really do make life wonderful for others, for those we love and care for.
Strategies: Call a friend,Listen to music,Play a video game,Read a character driven novel,Play a social video game,Read a poem you like aloud

Title: Support
Description: Somehow it is so much easier for us to experience support from others than it is to receive it from ourselves. Often it only takes a few encouraging words from a friend. We just want to hear that we are capable, and competent. We want to hear that others believe our goals are meaningful and deserve to be accomplished. It is striking how difficult it is to encourage oneself, to believe for ourself that our goals are attainable and deserve to be accomplished. Often others have skills that we think would help make our goals actualize and we believe that if our ideas really were good ones then others would want to lend their skills as well. It can be hard to give others space to have many possible needs that they are wanting to tend to, instead of letting our minds assume the worse, assuming that people cannot help us because they do not care or they do not believe in our vision.
Strategies: Call a friend,Call a parent,Floor starfish,Pillow nest,Name support options,Name one help to ask

Title: Consideration
Description:
I experience this as a sort of social confusion around what one is needing. I sometimes think that others may be trying to make my life wonderful but they are doing it without first having made contact with what need is alive in me. So maybe they are trying to contribute to my need for support or accomplishment when really want I’m needing is connection or just to be heard. How I wish they had slowed down and given me room to share what I was needing. 
Interestingly I find that tending to the need for consideration in others sometimes is the most reliable strategy for me to tend to the very same need in me. Perhaps that experience is also indicative of the reality that we all share in the same Life -- such that serving life in anyone ultimately serves Life in all of us.
Strategies: Call a friend,Volunteering / Acts of Kindness,Ask for a pause,Ask for channel shift,Three breaths before reply

Title: Need for all living things to flourish
Description: It can bring up great pain when our need for nurturing is not being met. We might think somehow we are to blame. Sometimes when we see suffering in other living things we experience pain that they are not being cared for or nurtured well. We might also feel it in us when someone’s behavior did not meet our need to be nurtured and/or considered.
Strategies: Tend to a plant,Share your strategies!
Original Claim: Concern that extends beyond the self supports sustainable systems. This need motivates stewardship, protection of vulnerable beings, and choices oriented toward long-term viability. Attending to broad flourishing links personal meaning with planetary health.
Supporting Sources:
https://gsdrc.org/document-library/what-is-the-evidence-on-the-effectiveness-of-empowerment-to-improve-health/ (WHO summary by Wallerstein: empowering communities to care for all members yields better collective outcomes)
https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/caring-for-others-can-bring-benefits.html (APS Observer: caring for others – even beyond one’s immediate circle – provides personal health and happiness benefits)
Rewritten Claim: Humans can feel a profound need to care about the well-being of all living things (not just ourselves or our immediate family). This expansive concern – often encompassing other people, future generations, animals, and the environment – encourages behaviors like environmental stewardship (taking care of nature), protecting those who are vulnerable, and making choices with long-term sustainability in mind. Psychologically, contributing to the greater good or the “flourishing” of a broad community can give individuals a strong sense of purpose and fulfillment. For example, studies show that volunteers in conservation or social justice efforts often report increased happiness and lower stress, as their altruistic actions feed back into their own well-being. Moreover, when many people adopt this ethos of caring beyond themselves, societies become more sustainable and resilient (e.g., communities are healthier and ecosystems more balanced). In essence, nurturing a concern for the flourishing of all life connects personal meaning with the health of our planet and society, creating a virtuous cycle between individual purpose and collective well-being.

Title: Inclusion
Description: What a profound experience it can be to have our need for inclusion met and how profoundly painful it can be to have it going unmet. We so want to be known as we are, to be seen completely, and accepted. We want to know we have a place in this world. We went to know that we really do make life wonderful for others and for those we love and care for.
Strategies: Try Meetup,Play a video game
Original Claim: Exclusion carries measurable psychological and physiological costs; inclusive norms counteract those risks. This need motivates widening participation, adjusting access, and designing for difference. Inclusion increases creativity and collective intelligence.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5729577/ (review noting loneliness and social exclusion can harm immune function and mental health; inclusive practices improve outcomes)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-39922-9 (2023 Scientific Reports study: diversity with inclusion significantly boosts team creativity and collective intelligence)
Rewritten Claim: Being excluded or marginalized isn’t just emotionally painful – it’s also linked to real psychological and even physical health harms (for example, chronic social isolation can raise stress hormones and weaken the immune system). By contrast, fostering inclusion – ensuring everyone feels they belong and can participate fully – helps to eliminate those risks. The need for inclusion drives efforts to open opportunities to a broader range of people, adapt environments to be accessible, and consciously embrace differences rather than treat them as obstacles. Research confirms that inclusive groups are more innovative and intelligent collectively: for instance, diverse teams only reach their highest creativity when the environment is truly inclusive and every member’s contributions are valued. Moreover, inclusive norms (where no one is left out due to who they are) create a sense of psychological safety that benefits all. In sum, inclusion not only prevents the personal damage of exclusion but actively improves group performance and creativity by leveraging everyone’s talents and perspectives.

Title: Community
Description: What a powerful experience it can be for us when our need for community is met. To experience inclusion, belonging, and often a sense of a purpose greater than any single person. There can be a lot of pain in even admitting to ourselves that we have this need for community that wants to be included in our strategies. It can be overwhelming to us. As if it is an insurmountable task to tend to this need.
Strategies: Try Meetup,Play a video game,Kind comment online
Original Claim: Cooperative groups have been the primary context of human survival and culture. This need motivates joining, contributing, and maintaining shared identity and mutual aid. Healthy community distributes risk and multiplies capacity.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6232274/ (anthropological perspective on humans as ultra-social, surviving via community cooperation)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2020/05/cover-empathy (APA article on how community and mutual aid improve resilience and well-being)
Rewritten Claim: Throughout evolutionary history, humans survived and thrived by banding together in cooperative communities – living in a group afforded protection, division of labor, and cultural growth. Reflecting this legacy, people have a fundamental need for community: we’re driven to join with others, contribute to group efforts, and uphold a shared identity that fosters belonging. In a well-functioning community, members help each other, which spreads out risks (for example, if one person falters, others can support them) and vastly increases the group’s overall capabilities (many hands and minds working together can achieve more than one alone). Research in social and evolutionary psychology underscores that strong social networks and communal ties improve individuals’ health and resilience. In short, a healthy community acts as a safety net and force multiplier, explaining why humans instinctively seek and value group belonging and mutual aid.

Title: Safety
Description: The childhood instinct to hide under the covers or run to the arms of a caregiver are both manifestations of our basic need for safety. It also very naturally includes the needs of others in our life. Seeing someone else in an unsafe situation also does not meet our need for safety therefore motivating us to find ways to tend to them.
Strategies: Crunch the numbers,Stare off,Self holding,Snuggle a pet,Road trip,Watch a comfort show,Back to wall lean,Butterfly taps,Hand on heart breaths,Floor starfish,5-4-3-2-1 check,Feel your feet,Wrap in a blanket,Name support options
Original Claim: Threat detection and protection are conserved across species and remain foundational for human functioning. This need motivates building stable environments, establishing boundaries, and choosing trustworthy relationships. With safety present, exploration and learning become viable.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2019/11/cover-safety (APA Monitor cover story on psychological safety: feeling safe is prerequisite for exploration, learning, and creativity)
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-017-0185-7 (study: perception of safety vs. threat alters cognitive processing and willingness to explore novel environments)
Rewritten Claim: The need for safety is deeply ingrained – across virtually all animals including humans, a sense of security (knowing one is not in immediate danger) is the foundation that allows normal functioning and growth. This need drives us to seek or create stable, secure environments: we set up physical safety (shelter, locks, safe neighborhoods), personal boundaries (so we won’t be harmed by others), and we gravitate towards people we trust. When we feel safe, our brains can devote resources to exploration, play, and learning new things; if we feel unsafe, those higher pursuits shut down in favor of focusing on survival. Psychologists note that children, for instance, only freely explore and learn when they feel securely attached and safe from harm. Similarly, adults in a workplace are most innovative when the climate is psychologically safe (no fear of humiliation or attack). In sum, safety is the platform upon which we build everything else – ensuring safety first makes it possible for individuals to venture out, take reasonable risks, and develop.

Title: Contribution
Description: I sometimes think of "contribution" as a bridge into the needs of others. We sometimes just genuinely wants to make life wonderful for others but we are terrified that we do not know how. What if we get it wrong? What if we try to make life wonderful for them but end up just making things worse? It can sometimes leave us paralyzed at the prospect. Nevertheless, our basic human need for contribution I find among the most obviously beautiful needs we have.
Strategies: Listen,Share your strategies!,Play a video game,Request a clear request,Charity work,Kind comment online,Name one help to ask
Original Claim: Contributing to something beyond oneself enhances purpose and cohesion. This need motivates service, knowledge-sharing, and creative work that benefits others. Channeling contribution converts personal energy into collective gains.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2020/09/doing-good-boosts-health (APA press release on how prosocial behavior and contributing to others increases sense of purpose and even health)
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17439760.2014.910829 (study linking volunteerism and altruistic contribution to higher life satisfaction and sense of meaning)
Rewritten Claim: People have a fundamental desire to contribute to causes or communities larger than themselves – doing so often gives a deep sense of purpose and strengthens social bonds. This need for contribution fuels activities like volunteering, sharing one’s knowledge or skills freely, or creating something for the common good. Studies find that engaging in prosocial service (e.g., helping others or one’s community) can improve one’s own wellbeing and instill a stronger sense of meaning in life. Essentially, by channeling our time and energy into contributions that benefit others or society, we transform individual effort into collective good. This not only aids the group (collective gains) but also feeds back to the individual as feelings of fulfillment, belonging, and coherence with one’s values.

Title: Peer Respect
Strategies: Call a friend
Original Claim: Standing with equals on fair terms supports morale and cooperation. This need motivates demonstrating competence, acknowledging others, and addressing status threats constructively. Peer respect keeps teamwork functional and dignified.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5373634/ (study on workplace teams: mutual professional respect among peers correlates with higher morale and team performance)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2009-02221-005 (research on status management in groups: when members feel respected as equals, cooperation increases and conflicts are fewer)
Rewritten Claim: People want to be respected by their peers – treated as equal colleagues whose contributions and dignity are valued. When team members view each other with respect, it boosts everyone’s morale and willingness to cooperate. The need for peer respect drives individuals to prove their competence (so others will esteem them), to give credit and respect to fellow members in turn, and to handle any tensions about status or recognition in a fair, open way (rather than via put-downs or envy). Studies show that teams in which members feel respected and not talked down to tend to function better: they communicate more freely and have higher collective morale, which translates into better outcomes. Ensuring peer respect essentially means each person feels “I am valued here just as others are” – this feeling keeps collaboration working smoothly and maintains each person’s sense of dignity within the group.

Title: Respect
Strategies: Call a friend,View art that you connect to,Name a limit kindly,Mirror kindness,Choose a gentler word,Micro boundary
Original Claim: Mutual regard reduces conflict costs and supports equitable collaboration. This need motivates clear boundaries, considerate language, and acknowledgment of value. Respect maintains dignity and workable relationships.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2018/04/principles (APA on principles of civility/respect in the workplace: respectful treatment reduces conflicts and increases collaboration)
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0146167215586198 (research: feeling respected in a group is associated with fewer interpersonal conflicts and greater commitment to group goals)
Rewritten Claim: Everyone has a need to be respected – to be treated with basic dignity and consideration. When respect is mutual in a group, conflicts tend to be less frequent and less damaging, and people can work together more fairly and effectively. The need for respect manifests in actions like setting and honoring personal boundaries (not intruding or violating someone’s limits), using polite and considerate language (even when disagreeing), and routinely acknowledging each person’s worth or contributions. By maintaining an atmosphere of respect, groups avoid many of the hidden “costs” of conflict such as grudges, sabotage, or disengagement. Psychological research finds that individuals who feel respected by their peers or leaders are more likely to cooperate and stay committed, whereas feeling disrespected often leads to disengagement or aggression. In summary, respect is the oil that keeps the social machine running smoothly: it preserves each person’s dignity and thus enables relationships and collaborations to remain functional and positive even under strain.

Title: Autonomy
Description: Freedom to be oneself. Often we hope that others to give us this freedom but I find it’s also quite difficult to give this freedom to ourselves. It’s such a beautiful need when we see it in others so why is it so hard to see it’s beauty in us?
Strategies: Go on walk,Make a request in conversation,Make art,Write,Play a video game,Road trip,Sing,Translate a “should”,Micro-request to self,Needs → strategies map,Name a limit kindly,Ask for channel shift,Turn on Do Not Disturb,Phone face-down,One thing off today,Name what’s within control,Future-walk sketch,Micro boundary,Name a want & a don’t
Original Claim: Robust evidence (e.g., self-determination theory) identifies autonomy as a universal psychological nutrient for motivation and well-being. This need motivates expressing preferences, making self-directed decisions, and setting boundaries. When autonomy is supported, persistence and quality of engagement typically increase.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3602424/ (Self-Determination Theory review, highlighting autonomy as a basic need for well-being)
https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/SDT/documents/2000_RyanDeci_SDT.pdf (Deci & Ryan, 2000 – seminal paper on autonomy’s role in motivation)
Rewritten Claim: According to extensive research (for example, self-determination theory), autonomy – the sense of volition and choice in one’s actions – is a fundamental psychological need across cultures. People are strongly motivated to voice their preferences, make their own decisions, and establish personal boundaries. Studies show that when individuals have autonomy support (e.g. freedom to make choices or control their work), they generally display greater persistence, better performance, and higher well-being (see Deci & Ryan 2000, American Psychologist, for evidence that autonomy enhances motivation and engagement). In short, autonomy acts like a psychological “nutrient”: supporting a person’s need for self-direction tends to boost their motivation and the quality of their participation in activities.

Title: To be seen
Strategies: Write,View previous things you've written or made,Make art,Listen to music,Play a video game,Sing,Read a poem you like aloud
Original Claim: Social visibility confirms presence and role within a group. This need motivates showing up authentically and inviting acknowledgement. Being seen anchors identity and belonging.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/1357650X.2019.1618420 (study on social recognition: being “seen” or recognized in a group setting enhanced participants’ sense of belonging and role clarity)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2009-04350-005 (research on identity and visibility: individuals who felt invisible in their social groups reported lower well-being and weaker group identification)
Rewritten Claim: Beyond just hearing our words, there’s a human need to be seen by others – meaning others acknowledge our presence, recognize who we are, and validate our role in the group. Social visibility – when your peers or community notice you and treat you as a distinct person – helps solidify your sense of identity (“I am here and I matter in this group”). This need leads people to present themselves genuinely (so that what others see is one’s real self) and to seek forms of acknowledgment (a greeting, a nod to one’s contributions, etc.). Being seen is closely tied to feeling one belongs: studies indicate that when individuals feel “invisible” or overlooked in a group, it undermines their well-being and commitment, whereas being recognized and visible boosts their sense of belonging and self-esteem. In practice, small acts like using someone’s name, noticing their efforts, or giving them the spotlight can fulfill this need. When people are seen in these ways, it reinforces their membership in the community and “anchors” their identity as part of that social world.

Title: Acknowledgement
Strategies: Play a video game,Read a poem you like aloud
Original Claim: Recognizing contribution reinforces cooperative behavior in human groups. This need motivates requesting or offering specific feedback and making results visible. Reliable acknowledgement sustains morale and signals that effort matters.
Supporting Sources:
https://hbr.org/2016/05/why-recognizing-your-employees-is-the-easiest-way-to-boost-morale (HBR article on the impact of recognition on morale and cooperation)
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/job.2117 (research showing that acknowledgment and feedback increase teamwork and retention)
Rewritten Claim: Humans thrive on having their contributions noticed – acknowledging someone’s good work encourages them (and others) to keep cooperating. The need for acknowledgement drives people to seek and give meaningful feedback and to publicize achievements or results. Organizational studies find that when employees feel recognized for their efforts, their morale and engagement rise, which in turn reinforces cooperative behavior (see HBR, 2016: recognition boosts morale and performance). In practice, consistently acknowledging contributions shows individuals that their effort matters, thereby maintaining motivation and strengthening the group’s collaborative spirit.

Title: Appreciation
Strategies: View previous things you've written or made,View art that you connect to,Specific thank-you,Five gratitudes by need
Original Claim: Gratitude strengthens social bonds and increases prosocial behavior across cultures. This need motivates noticing value, naming what worked, and reciprocating care. Practiced appreciation maintains trust and energizes ongoing collaboration.
Supporting Sources:
https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/why_gratitude_is_good (summary of cross-cultural research on gratitude’s effects on relationships and prosocial behavior)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2012/01/happy (APA Monitor – “The Gratitude Effect” – describing how expressing thanks improves trust and social ties)
Rewritten Claim: Expressing and receiving gratitude is a powerful social glue – research shows that feeling appreciated or thanking others strengthens relationships and encourages people to act kindly in return (these effects are observed in many cultures). The need for appreciation leads us to notice what is valuable in others’ actions, explicitly acknowledge what went well, and respond to kindness with kindness. By regularly practicing gratitude and appreciation, groups build greater mutual trust and goodwill. In other words, showing appreciation not only affirms the recipient but also energizes ongoing cooperation, as people who feel valued are more likely to continue contributing positively.

Title: Trust
Strategies: Mindfulness (Trust),Schedule your day
Original Claim: Confidence in others’ intentions and competence reduces transaction costs and stress. This need motivates transparency, reliability, and incremental risk-taking. Trust enlarges what groups can do together.
Supporting Sources:
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022242910391365 (study: high trust in business or team relationships significantly lowers the costs of monitoring and coordination, improving performance)
https://www.apa.org/science/about/psa/2019/11/trust (APA Science brief: trust in others reduces stress responses in cooperative tasks and allows for greater risk-sharing leading to innovation)
Rewritten Claim: Trust is the belief that others have good intentions and are capable in their role – and it’s essential for smooth cooperation. When trust is present in a relationship or team, people don’t need to waste energy constantly watching their backs or double-checking everything, which lowers stress and “transaction costs” (the extra effort of dealing with doubt or verification). The need for trust drives behaviors like being open and transparent (so others know they’re not being deceived), being dependable (so others learn they can count on you), and gradually extending trust to others by taking small risks – for example, delegating a task and seeing it through. Research shows that in high-trust environments, groups can undertake more ambitious projects and adapt faster, because members willingly share information and responsibilities without fear. In essence, trust expands the scope of what people can achieve together: it’s like social glue that enables complex teamwork, innovation, and supportive relationships that would collapse if everyone was suspicious. Thus, nurturing trust by consistent honest behavior and mutual respect allows teams and communities to reach higher levels of collaboration with less friction.

Title: Dependability
Description: Defined as "the quality of being trustworthy and reliable" we ought to be careful to not mistake our evaluations of others as if they are our personal needs. Needs contain no reference to specific people taking specific action. Therefore a need like dependability is really rooted in concepts like predictability. We'd like to know that if we expect something to happen, that it will. When other's fail to do as they say they will do it therefore does not meet our needs. We don't have to level a new judgement of them in order to see that our own need was not met. Therefore, the tend to our need for dependability without reference to others may look something like making simple plans or creating a schedule. I could mean choosing a mindfulness meditation in which we allow ourselves to notice all the things that are predictable for us: like our breath, the rising and setting sun, our ability to lift our hand or blink our eyes when we choose to.
Strategies: Schedule your day,Mindfulness (Trust)
Original Claim: Reliability reduces monitoring costs and enables complex cooperation. This need motivates keeping agreements, building robust processes, and choosing trustworthy partners. Dependability is the infrastructure of interpersonal and institutional trust.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0749597818301940 (study on how reliability of team members lowers the need for oversight and improves collective performance)
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916837/ (research finding that people strongly prefer and trust those who are consistently honest/reliable)
Rewritten Claim: Each person has an optimal pace and style for doing work or learning. When we can operate at a pace that suits us (rather than being rushed or held back too much), we tend to learn more effectively and make fewer errors, and we can keep going longer without exhaustion. This need to “do it my own way, in my own time” leads people to tailor their schedules and break tasks into sequences that fit their natural rhythm. Research on job design indicates that employees who have control over the timing and method of their work – for example, setting their own task pace – experience less burnout and maintain higher quality performance. By respecting individuals’ pacing needs, organizations and educators can preserve quality of output and protect people’s well-being over the long term, since working in sync with one’s personal tempo reduces chronic stress.

Title: Honesty
Strategies: Listen to music,Write,View previous things you've written or made,Write three sentences,Observation only,Self-check scale,Name a want & a don’t
Original Claim: Transparent information enables accurate coordination and reduces relational risk. This need motivates factual clarity, timely disclosure, and correction of errors. Honesty is a stable basis for trust.
Supporting Sources:
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916837/ (study: people strongly prefer to trust those who show consistent honesty; honest behavior biases others to view one as trustworthy)
https://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/truth-hurts-honesty-relationship-health-316932/ (University of Rochester study: greater honesty in expressing needs or issues led to better relationship outcomes)
Rewritten Claim: Being honest – sharing truthful, clear information – is crucial for groups to coordinate their actions correctly and for individuals to feel secure with each other. When we have the full, accurate picture, we can make better decisions and avoid the hidden pitfalls that come with deception. The need for honesty pushes us to communicate facts plainly, to be forthcoming about important matters in a timely way, and to admit and fix mistakes rather than cover them up. Consistent honesty provides a foundation for trust: studies have shown that we are biased to trust people with a reputation for honesty, and in relationships, open truthful dialogue (even when discussing problems) leads to stronger, healthier outcomes. In essence, honesty creates predictability and safety in interactions – others know they can take one’s words at face value – making it a bedrock for any trusting relationship or cooperative effort.

Title: Honor
Strategies: (Honor) Reflection Meditation
Original Claim: Alignment with ethical standards protects reputation and group trust. This need motivates value-consistent choices, restraint, and repair after violations. Honor integrates personal integrity with communal expectations.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/honor-and-moral-development (discussion of honor as adherence to ethical norms and its role in group trust and reputation)
https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/releases/psp-pspi0000178.pdf (review on moral reputation: upholding moral standards maintains trust in groups)
Rewritten Claim: Honor involves living up to ethical principles and norms – essentially, it’s about having integrity that others recognize. This strengthens one’s reputation for being upright and fosters trust within the group. The need for honor drives individuals to make choices that are consistent with their professed values, to exercise restraint from unethical temptations, and to make amends if they do something that violates the moral code. By behaving honorably, a person aligns their personal integrity with what their community expects ethically. Research in social psychology suggests that when people consistently act according to moral standards, they earn trust and esteem from others. Conversely, dishonorable actions (lies, cheating) can damage one’s reputation and erode group trust. In short, honor acts as a bridge between the individual and the community: it ensures that personal behavior upholds communal ethical expectations, thereby protecting both the individual’s good name and the group’s mutual trust.

Title: Commitment
Description: Relationships are often the first things that come to mind when we notice our need for commitment isn't being met. Interestingly, however, we often fail to keep commitments to ourselves too. In this way making small attainable plans/commitments to ourselves can be a healthy way to tend to this need without references to others. During a meltdown I once committed to myself that I would flip my hand over on the count of three. In it's own tiny way I was able to prove to myself that I do have some control over myself and that I can predict the future even if it's just in this tiny way.
Strategies: Schedule your day,Crunch the numbers
Original Claim: Stable investment in people and projects allows long-term goals to be realized. This need motivates planning, prioritizing, and sustaining effort across setbacks. Sound commitment breeds reliability and shared momentum.
Supporting Sources:
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1997-04604-006 (research on commitment in relationships and teams contributing to long-term success and trust)

The need for equality drives efforts to even out imbalances: for instance, ensuring everyone’s voice is heard, adjusting rules or resource allocation to be fair, and keeping an eye on outcomes to catch inequalities. Studies on procedural justice show that when people perceive a process as fair and inclusive (everyone gets a say), they are more likely to cooperate and accept group decisions, and less likely to feel resentment. Moreover, environments that value equality and inclusion help create psychological safety – members feel safe to express themselves without fear, which further improves team innovation and trust. Ultimately, emphasizing equality not only enhances the legitimacy of leadership or decisions (because they’re seen as fair) but also fosters a climate where individuals feel respected and united, reducing friction and enabling better group performance.

Title: Empowerment
Strategies: Listen to music,Sing,Stand Largely

https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/6/2/e010425 (study linking patient empowerment with improved health management and resilience)
Rewritten Claim: Feeling empowered – that is, being capable and having the means to influence one’s circumstances – tends to make people more resilient and improves their life outcomes, including health. This need for empowerment drives efforts like developing one’s skills, participating in decisions that affect oneself (instead of being a passive recipient), and knocking down unnecessary obstacles that limit people’s agency. Public health and community research has shown that when individuals or groups are empowered (given knowledge, resources, and a voice), they often experience better well-being and can cope with challenges more effectively. In essence, empowerment broadens the realm of possibilities – it enables both individuals and communities to achieve more because they have the confidence and capacity to act on their goals. For example, an empowered patient manages their illness better, and an empowered community finds local solutions to problems, each leading to healthier, more positive outcomes.

Title: Consistency
Strategies: Schedule your day
Original Claim: Predictable patterns free attention for creativity and problem solving. This need motivates establishing routines, standards, and stable cues. Consistency provides a dependable platform for growth.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1359432X.2018.1531670 (study showing that consistent routines reduce cognitive load and errors, enabling more creative work)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2002-15408-004 (research on how environmental consistency and predictable structure benefit learning and innovation)
Rewritten Claim: When certain aspects of life or work are consistent and predictable, our minds are freed up to focus on higher-level tasks like creative thinking or complex problem-solving. This need for consistency leads people to create routines, set standards, and use stable signals or processes in their environment. For example, a consistent daily schedule or a standard method for tasks can reduce uncertainty and mental effort, leaving more brainpower for innovation. Psychological research supports this: having predictable frameworks (and fewer random surprises) lowers stress and mistakes, providing a solid platform from which individuals or teams can safely experiment and grow (see research on routine and creativity showing that structured time encourages more creative output once the basics are handled). In essence, consistency in key areas offers dependability, which then nurtures confidence to explore and develop in new areas.

Title: Genuineness
Strategies: Listen to music
Original Claim: Straightforward signaling prevents confusion and builds credibility. This need motivates honest disclosure, consistency between words and actions, and corrective feedback. Genuineness maintains clear, dependable relationships.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1090513817303000 (study indicating that straightforward, sincere communication builds interpersonal credibility and trust)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2019-13350-001 (findings that inconsistency between words and actions erodes trust; authenticity fosters clear communication)
Rewritten Claim: Being genuine means communicating in a straightforward, truthful way and ensuring our actions match our words. This clarity in signaling one’s intentions or feelings greatly reduces confusion in relationships and helps others know they can trust what we say. The need for genuineness drives us to be honest and transparent, to strive for alignment between what we profess and what we actually do, and to give or seek candid feedback when things don’t match up. Research on trust formation confirms that people who are perceived as straight shooters (no hidden agenda, no deceit) earn more credibility and maintain stronger relationships. In contrast, if someone’s words and actions diverge frequently, it creates doubt and misunderstanding. Therefore, practicing genuineness keeps relationships clear and dependable – everyone knows where they stand with each other.

Title: Mattering

Supporting Sources:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5328651/ (study: higher sense of mattering to family or community correlates with better well-being and motivation)
Rewritten Claim: “Mattering” refers to feeling that you truly matter to other people – that you are noticed, cared about, and valued by them. Research indicates that when individuals feel they matter to others, they experience better mental health and are more engaged and motivated in their daily lives. This need to feel significant drives people to seek roles or tasks that are meaningful and valued by their group, to look for feedback that their contributions have an impact, and to get involved in situations where their presence makes a difference. In environments (workplaces, schools, families) that consciously affirm each person’s significance, both the individual and the group benefit: individuals gain a sense of purpose and commitment, and groups enjoy higher participation and loyalty. In summary, making sure people know they matter – that their existence and input are important – reinforces a shared sense of purpose and boosts overall well-being and engagement.

Title: Rest
Strategies: Smell something,Stare off,Play a video game,No Man's Sky,4-7-8 breathing,Legs up the wall,Floor starfish,Two-minute eye rest,Wrap in a blanket,Pillow nest
Original Claim: Periodic disengagement and sleep consolidate memory and repair biological systems. This need motivates protecting sleep windows and creating low-demand intervals. Adequate rest sustains clarity, mood, and health.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/why-sleep-matters-beyond-brain (NIH summary: sleep is vital for memory consolidation, metabolic regulation, immune function, etc.)
https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about_sleep/why_sleep.html (CDC: adequate sleep improves mood, cognitive performance, and reduces health risks)
Rewritten Claim: Rest – especially quality sleep and regular breaks – is non-negotiable for a healthy mind and body. During sleep and true rest, our brains organize and solidify memories and our body performs critical maintenance like tissue repair and immune system regulation. The need for rest drives behaviors such as setting aside enough hours for sleep, defending those sleep times from interruptions, and taking short daily pauses or days off where we aren’t under pressure to perform. Extensive medical research confirms that people who get sufficient sleep and downtime think more clearly, maintain better mood stability, and have stronger overall health (for example, chronic sleep deprivation is linked to concentration problems, irritability, and higher risk of illnesses like hypertension and depression). Protecting rest time – whether it’s a good night’s sleep or a relaxing afternoon off – ensures we can sustain our mental clarity, emotional balance, and physical well-being in the long run.

Title: Mutuality
Strategies: Call a friend,Make a request in conversation,Ask for a pause,One kind text,Name one help to ask
Original Claim: Balanced exchange prevents burnout and resentment in ongoing relationships. This need motivates negotiation of roles, explicit reciprocity, and rebalancing when loads shift. Mutuality maintains dignity and stability on all sides.
Supporting Sources:
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/pere.12051 (research on mutuality in long-term relationships: reciprocal support and balanced give-and-take linked to relationship satisfaction and lower burnout for caregivers)
https://www.jstor.org/stable/585524 (social exchange theory: relationships with balanced exchange of support have greater stability and equity)
Rewritten Claim: In any long-term relationship (personal or professional), both parties need to give and receive in a roughly balanced way to keep things healthy – if one side does all the giving and the other all the taking, it often leads to exhaustion or bitterness. The need for mutuality drives people to negotiate and clarify roles (so one person isn’t unknowingly carrying more burden), to practice reciprocity (“I’ll help you this time, and I trust you’ll help me when I need it”), and to readjust arrangements when circumstances change (for example, if one partner gets sick, the other might take on more temporarily, with the understanding of mutual support). When relationships operate on mutuality – fair two-way exchange – everyone’s dignity is respected and the relationship stays stable and satisfying. Studies in social psychology find that perceived fairness and mutual support in a relationship correlate with higher trust and longevity of that relationship. In summary, mutuality ensures no one chronically feels exploited or drained; instead, all sides feel supported and valued, which sustains the bond over time.

Title: Relaxation
Strategies: Play a video game,No Man's Sky
Original Claim: Deliberate down-shifting restores cognitive flexibility and interpersonal patience. This need motivates quiet leisure, gentle movement, and mind-uncluttering practices. Relaxation renews capacity for sustained effort.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02146/full (study: brief relaxation techniques improved executive function and reduced stress, indicating cognitive benefits)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2013/10/relaxation (APA Monitor article on how relaxation practices like deep breathing, walking in nature, etc., replenish mental reserves and improve patience and focus)
Rewritten Claim: Intentionally slowing down and engaging in relaxing activities is crucial for our mental flexibility and social patience. When we never pause, our minds and tempers can get brittle – but deliberate relaxation (like taking a quiet break, doing light exercise or yoga, meditating, hobbies, etc.) helps clear mental clutter and resets our capacity to think creatively and deal calmly with others. The need for relaxation drives us to carve out leisure time, enjoy soothing or fun low-pressure activities, and practice techniques that calm the mind. Research shows that even short relaxation exercises can restore cognitive functions like working memory and self-control that are depleted by stress. After truly relaxing, people often find they can sustain effort and concentration for longer periods again and are less irritable in their interactions. In essence, relaxation isn’t idleness – it’s a necessary renewal process. By regularly down-shifting from high gear, we actually improve our overall productivity and the quality of our engagements when we return to our tasks or relationships.

Title: Closeness
Strategies: Call a friend,Cuddle your favorite stuffed animal,Call a parent
Original Claim: Attachment theory and cross-cultural research identify emotionally attuned proximity as protective for development and stress recovery. This need motivates shared time, attentive presence, and mutual responsiveness. Closeness strengthens resilience through co-regulation and trust.
Supporting Sources:
https://cpa.ca/attachment-in-children/ (Canadian Psychological Association – secure attachment helps children cope with stress and fosters healthy development)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2013/06/social-deception (research on co-regulation: close relationships buffer stress responses)
Rewritten Claim: Psychologists (starting with attachment theory) have found that having someone emotionally in-tune and physically or emotionally close is a powerful buffer for stress and a boon for healthy development. In other words, feeling closely connected – for example through shared quality time, attentive listening, and responsive care – protects people (especially children) by helping them regulate their emotions with support from another person (a process called co-regulation). This need for closeness drives us to seek warm, reliable relationships. Secure attachment in childhood is linked to better coping with fear and stress, and even in adults, social support from a loved one can calm the body’s stress responses. By cultivating closeness and trust, individuals become more resilient: they recover faster from adversity and gain confidence knowing someone “has their back.”

Title: Authenticity
Strategies: Play a video game,Write
Original Claim: Congruence between inner experience and outer behavior supports clarity and reduces social ambiguity. This need motivates transparent communication and value-consistent choices. Respecting authenticity preserves self-coherence and dependable signaling in relationships.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/15298868.2013.838904 (study finding authenticity is linked to higher self-esteem and better relationship satisfaction)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2006-06108-007 (research on how behaving in line with one’s true self reduces stress and confusion in social interactions)
Rewritten Claim: Living and interacting in a way that aligns with one’s true feelings and values (i.e. being authentic) provides clarity for oneself and others. When our outward behavior matches our inner experience, it minimizes confusion or mixed signals in social situations. This need for authenticity drives honest, transparent communication and decisions that reflect our core values. Psychological research suggests that people who act authentically tend to experience greater self-esteem and more satisfying relationships, likely because others can trust that their signals are genuine. In summary, honoring authenticity helps maintain personal integrity and ensures more dependable, clear interactions in relationships.

Title: Self expression
Strategies: Play an instrument,Write,Make art,Listen to music,No Man's Sky,Sing
Original Claim: Externalizing inner experience clarifies thinking and supports mutual understanding. This need motivates writing, speaking, making, or otherwise communicating authentically. Expression integrates identity and connects people.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10400419.2018.1446747 (study on creative self-expression: writing/artistic expression improved cognitive processing of emotions and identity coherence)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2017/07/art-therapy (APA article: expressing oneself through words or art can lead to personal insights and improved communication with others)
Rewritten Claim: Humans have a strong need to express what’s inside of them – their thoughts, feelings, ideas – in some outward form. By putting inner experiences into external form (through language, art, music, movement, or any creative act), we often understand ourselves better and also enable others to understand us. This need for self-expression drives people to journal or write, to speak up and share their perspective, to create art or projects that reflect their inner world, and generally to communicate in ways that feel true to themselves. Research has shown that such authentic expression can clarify one’s thinking and emotions (for instance, writing about a stressful experience often brings new insights and relief). Moreover, when we express ourselves and are heard or seen, it affirms our identity and builds bridges to other people – they can connect with the real “us.” In summary, self-expression is both an individual integrator (helping us make sense of who we are) and a social connector (allowing others to know us), making it a vital component of psychological well-being and interpersonal bonding.

Title: Integrity
Strategies: Write,Translate a “should”,Micro boundary,Value compass card
Original Claim: Coherence between values and behavior reduces internal conflict and external confusion. This need motivates alignment, boundary maintenance, and principled action under pressure. Integrity supports self-respect and predictability for others.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.apa.org/ethics/moral-integrity (APA discussion on moral integrity: acting consistently with one’s values yields psychological coherence and social trust)
https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-70772-2_7 (analysis of integrity in leadership: leaders who align actions with values gain respect and provide clear, predictable direction)
Rewritten Claim: Integrity means living by your principles – making sure that what you do reflects what you deeply believe is right. When people have integrity, they experience less inner turmoil (because they aren’t betraying their own values) and they avoid confusing those around them (because their behavior consistently matches their stated ideals). The need for integrity drives individuals to align their decisions and actions with their core values, to maintain personal boundaries that prevent compromising those values, and to stick to ethics even when under pressure to do otherwise. This consistency supports self-respect (you can feel at peace with yourself) and makes one’s behavior more predictable and trustworthy to others. For example, a leader with integrity will act according to their professed mission and moral standards even in tough situations, which earns them respect and makes it easier for others to anticipate their actions. In short, integrity is about wholeness of character – it ensures we are the same person in principle and practice, benefiting both our inner well-being and our relationships.

Title: Empathy
Strategies: View previous things you've written or made

This need motivates perspective-taking, reflective listening, and iterative checking for understanding. Practiced well, it reduces misinterpretation and supports relational alignment.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1115402/full (study showing empathy and communication skills improve team coordination and performance)
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1754073917708615 (research on how empathy reduces conflict and misunderstanding in relationships)
Rewritten Claim: Empathy – the ability to understand and share what another person is feeling or thinking – is crucial for working smoothly with others and for fixing relationship problems. Being truly empathetic motivates us to put ourselves in others’ shoes, listen carefully to what they say, and double-check that we’re understanding them correctly. By doing so, we greatly cut down on misinterpretations and friction. For example, studies have found that teams with higher empathy and better communication have more cohesion and perform better because members anticipate each other’s needs and clarify potential confusion. (It’s worth noting that different people may need different approaches for empathy; for instance, some autistic individuals prefer very clear, concrete communication to feel understood.) In practice, cultivating empathy leads to better “relational alignment” – everyone feels heard and on the same page, which improves coordination and conflict resolution.

Title: Privacy

Supporting Sources:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5579245/ (research on digital age privacy: control over personal information and the ability to be alone correlate with better stress regulation and autonomy)
Rewritten Claim: Privacy – having time and space to oneself and control over one’s personal information – is essential for maintaining a sense of autonomy and for mental processing. We need moments of seclusion, away from outside observation or demands, to reflect on our experiences, consolidate our thoughts, and simply recharge. This need for privacy leads people to sometimes withdraw (e.g., closing the door, taking a solo walk), to share personal information selectively (choosing who knows what about one’s life), and to set up physical or digital boundaries (like curtains, passwords) that delineate a personal zone. Research indicates that such private downtime supports introspection and helps individuals integrate their experiences into a coherent sense of self. Additionally, feeling in control of one’s information (not constantly surveilled or exposed) has been linked to reduced stress and greater well-being. In summary, privacy gives individuals the protected space needed for self-definition and recovery, ultimately enabling them to engage with others more fully after emerging from that space.

Title: Order
Strategies: Clean something,Schedule your day,Parking-lot note,Calendar one thing,Mark a date on a calendar,Put it on paper
Original Claim: Structure and organization reduce error and cognitive strain. This need motivates sorting, sequencing, standardizing, and documenting. Order frees attention for creativity and nuanced thinking.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0003687012000588 (study: organized workspaces and structured information reduce mistakes and mental overload)
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2012.02153.x (research showing that induced physical order (tidiness) can improve people’s executive function and decision-making, presumably by lowering distraction)
Rewritten Claim: Having order – a sense of organized structure in our environment or tasks – helps us function with fewer errors and less mental effort. When things are sorted, in their proper sequence, standardized where appropriate, and documented clearly, we don’t waste brainpower trying to find things or figure out chaotic situations. This need for order drives us to tidy up, make checklists or schedules, establish routines, and write down procedures. By reducing clutter and unpredictability, orderliness actually increases our capacity for higher-level thinking: with basic details under control, our attention is “freed up” for creativity, problem-solving, or subtle analysis. Empirical studies have found that people in an organized setting tend to perform better on complex cognitive tasks and make more prudent decisions than those in a messy or unstructured setting (disorder imposes a cognitive tax). In summary, maintaining order mitigates unnecessary cognitive strain and distraction, providing a stable platform from which we can engage in more nuanced or inventive thinking.

Title: Beauty
Strategies: Clean something,Go on walk,Play a video game,Read a poem you like aloud,Trace an object,Open the blinds

Supporting Sources:

https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797612464121 (study linking exposure to aesthetically pleasing natural environments with cognitive benefits and stress reduction)
Rewritten Claim: Humans naturally respond to beauty – we’re attuned to patterns and harmony in our environment, which historically signaled things like safety or rich resources (for example, a lush, orderly landscape might promise food and shelter). As a result, we have a drive to seek out nature, art, and pleasing design that help us feel oriented and at ease. Psychology research confirms that exposure to beautiful natural settings can restore our ability to concentrate, lift our mood, and reduce stress hormones. In practice, “investing in beauty” – whether by spending time in nature or creating aesthetically pleasing spaces – tends to improve mental focus, promote calmness, and provide a restorative experience for our minds.

Title: Control
Strategies: Play a video game,Road trip,Schedule your day,Sing
Original Claim: Influence over conditions reduces threat and improves outcomes in uncertain environments. This need motivates setting parameters, using contingency plans, and shaping contexts. Appropriate control promotes safety and effective agency.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.jstor.org/stable/20627226 (research on locus of control: having control or influence correlates with reduced stress and better task outcomes)
https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/about/social-ecologicalmodel.html (CDC commentary on how controlling one’s environment reduces perceived threats and fosters safety – related to public health contexts)
Rewritten Claim: Having some degree of control over our circumstances makes uncertainty less frightening and often leads to better results. We all have a need to feel we can influence what happens to us. This drives us to set limits or rules, prepare backup plans (“if X, then Y”), and actively shape our surroundings rather than be passive. Studies on “locus of control” show that when people feel they have control over a situation, they experience less stress and perform better, whereas a lack of control can trigger threat responses (learned helplessness, etc.). By exerting appropriate control – not in an overbearing way but enough to steer key factors – individuals create safer conditions and can act more effectively. In summary, some control over one’s environment or outcomes bolsters a sense of security and enables more confident, purposeful action.

Title: Predictability
Strategies: Schedule your day,Calendar one thing
Original Claim: Reliable patterns make planning possible and reduce vigilance. This need motivates clear schedules, transparent protocols, and advance notice of change. Predictability stabilizes attention and performance.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10615806.2019.1640981 (study: unpredictability in environment increases stress and hyper-vigilance; predictable routines reduce stress response)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2017/07-08/peace-mind (APA Monitor: the importance of routine and predictability for mental focus and reduced anxiety)
Rewritten Claim: People feel more at ease and can concentrate better when their environment and schedule are predictable. Knowing what to expect – having reliable patterns – means we don’t have to be on high alert all the time, and we can plan our actions with confidence. The need for predictability drives us to create clear timetables, establish transparent procedures or rules, and give advance warnings before changes happen. For example, a workplace that communicates its schedule and any upcoming shifts well in advance allows employees to focus on their tasks instead of worrying about surprises. Research in stress psychology confirms that unpredictability is a significant stressor (uncertain situations make our brains more vigilant and anxious), whereas predictable contexts lower baseline stress and improve cognitive performance. Thus, predictability in our routines and systems provides a stable backdrop that steadies attention and supports consistent performance.

Title: Accomplishment
Strategies: Clean something,Play a video game,Crunch the numbers,Make art,Make a list and check things off
Original Claim: Mastery and efficacy are intrinsically rewarding and have clear adaptive value in variable environments. This need motivates goal formation, deliberate practice, and tracking progress. Honoring accomplishment channels effort into competence that benefits both the individual and the group.
Supporting Sources:
https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2014-37155-001.html (Self-determination theory research: competence/mastery as a basic psychological need)
https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00304/full (review on intrinsic reward of mastery and skill development)
Rewritten Claim: Humans are driven to achieve mastery in skills and tasks – accomplishing goals and feeling effective is inherently satisfying and also advantageous for survival in changing environments. This need for achievement leads people to set goals, engage in focused practice, and measure their progress. Psychological studies on intrinsic motivation confirm that developing competence (becoming skilled and effective) is rewarding in itself and encourages ongoing effort. By pursuing and recognizing accomplishments, individuals build valuable skills that not only enhance their own capabilities but also contribute to group success (e.g., a well-practiced skill can be shared or used to aid the community). In short, valuing accomplishment helps channel effort into growing one’s competence, yielding benefits for both the person and those around them.

Title: Physical Fitness
Strategies: Reduce Mental Tasks
Original Claim: Capacity for movement underpins health, safety, and daily functioning. This need motivates activity, strength and endurance practices, and balanced recovery. Fitness supports mood, cognition, and independence.
Supporting Sources:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1470658/ (study linking physical fitness with better brain health and functional independence in older adults)
Rewritten Claim: Humans have a basic need to stay physically fit – to be capable of movement and exertion – because it is fundamental to health and everyday living. This need drives us to engage in physical activities: practices that build strength, endurance, flexibility, as well as to incorporate rest and recovery for balance. A good level of fitness boosts our mood (exercise is known to release endorphins and reduce anxiety), enhances cognitive function (fit individuals often have better memory and executive function), and helps maintain independence as we age (by preventing frailty and reducing injury risk). Public health research indicates that regular physical activity is associated with numerous benefits: from improved safety (stronger muscles can prevent falls, for example) to better management of chronic conditions and sharper mental performance. In short, tending to our physical fitness needs keeps our bodies and minds in shape, enabling us to navigate daily tasks safely and enjoy a higher quality of life.

Title: Acceptance
Strategies: Play an instrument,Write,Make art,Unsended appreciation,Name what’s outside control
Original Claim: In social species, inclusion confers safety and access to resources, so human attention is highly tuned to signals of being welcomed as we are. This need motivates seeking contexts where differences are received without correction, inviting feedback, and building norms that reduce social threat. Valuing acceptance sustains psychological security and strengthens long-term cooperation.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237344651_Social_Inclusion_Facilitates_Interest_in_Mating (evolutionary psychology study noting that social acceptance cues indicate safety and resource sharing)
https://www.apa.org/monitor/2019/05/ce-corner-isolation (APA article discussing the psychological and physiological costs of social exclusion)
Rewritten Claim: Humans have evolved to seek acceptance because being included in a group historically offered protection and resource sharing (e.g. group living provided safety from predators and pooled resources). We are highly sensitive to cues of inclusion or rejection, which motivates us to find environments where we are genuinely welcomed without undue criticism. Fostering a climate of acceptance – where differences are respected and feedback is constructive – contributes to a sense of psychological security and promotes cooperation over the long term (see https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316 for survival benefits of social bonds). In short, valuing acceptance helps individuals feel safe and supports enduring collaborative relationships.

Title: Growth
Strategies: Play a video game,Make art,Play an instrument,Write,Read one paragraph

Supporting Sources:
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2015-46007-001 (research on “growth mindset” showing that embracing challenges and learning from feedback leads to greater skill development and adaptability)
https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2017/10/brain-adapt-learning (APA press release on how the brain physically adapts when we continually learn new things, improving cognitive flexibility)
Rewritten Claim: Humans are built to learn and adapt – continuous growth (whether in knowledge, skills, or personal development) is a driving force behind both our individual life progress and the advancement of our societies. The need for growth makes us seek out feedback on how we’re doing, devote time to practice and mastery of new abilities, and take on incrementally bigger challenges as we improve. Psychological studies on learning orientation (e.g., having a “growth mindset”) show that people who focus on growth by learning from mistakes and pushing their skills tend to become more flexible thinkers and achieve higher competence over time. Valuing growth means you’re less stagnant and more prepared for change: by constantly updating and expanding your capacities, you stay adaptable. In summary, prioritizing growth – always learning and evolving – enhances one’s long-term abilities and resilience in a changing world.

Title: Security
Strategies: Watch a comfort show,Crunch the numbers
Original Claim: Resource and relationship stability allow planning and long-term investment. This need motivates saving, redundancy, and dependable support networks. Security frees attention for growth and creativity.
Supporting Sources:
https://www.jstor.org/stable/41428503 (study on financial and relationship security: having secure baseline resources correlates with better long-term planning and higher creativity)
https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2018-13314-006 (research: when basic security needs are met, individuals are more likely to pursue self-actualization goals like creativity and personal growth – consistent with Maslow’s hierarchy)
Rewritten Claim: Security means having a stable base – like steady resources (financial, food, shelter) and reliable relationships – such that you’re not constantly worried about losing the essentials. This stability enables people to plan for the future and invest time or resources into long-term goals. The need for security drives behaviors such as saving money or supplies for a “rainy day,” building in redundancies or backup plans to guard against unforeseen loss, and developing dependable support networks (family, community, insurance) that can catch you if you fall. Research in psychology and economics suggests that when individuals feel secure about their basic needs and relationships, their minds are freed up to be more creative, take strategic risks, and focus on personal growth or complex problem-solving. By contrast, if someone is in an insecure situation (unsure if they’ll have food next week or if their job is stable), much of their mental energy gets diverted to anxiety and short-term survival thinking. Therefore, attaining a level of security essentially unlocks higher-order capacities – it provides peace of mind that allows attention to shift from merely surviving to thriving.
